messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

The stalking began quietly. A stranger she had briefly exchanged words with at a neighborhood café began appearing on her bicycle commute home. At first, it was coincidence—she told herself. Then he was outside her building, on the same bike, watching. He followed her for weeks, always on that bicycle, never speaking, never close enough to confront. She reported him, but without identifiable threats or direct contact, the police filed it as suspicious behavior, not a crime. He was never charged. She moved to a new apartment across town, but the damage had already taken root.

As a graphic designer, she now works in a bustling open-plan studio downtown. Every day, she enters the office and instinctively takes a desk near the emergency exit, always facing the door. If a coworker approaches from behind, her body tenses before her mind registers the sound. She scans the room repeatedly, cataloging faces, bags, anything unusual. On a recent walk during lunch break, a parked bicycle a block away made her freeze, heart hammering, before she realized it was just a bike leaning against a rack. These startle reactions—false alarms—happen several times a week. She has come to believe that the world is simply dangerous, that people are not what they seem, and most of all that the person who stalked her faced no consequences. This injustice feels like a permanent stain on her sense of safety.

Her husband notices she no longer wants to go to the park or walk to the corner store. She avoids the neighborhood where the stalker first appeared, but her avoidance has spread: she now checks her surroundings before leaving any building, and she maps escape routes even in familiar places like the grocery store. The more she scans, the more potential threats she spots—a man walking too slowly, a cyclist approaching from behind—and each one reinforces her belief that she cannot trust her environment. She feels certain that if she lets her guard down, something terrible will happen. This vigilance also feeds back into her threat system: her constant planning and checking keep her on edge, so a sudden noise or a bicycle whizzing past triggers a full startle response, as if the danger were immediate.

She has begun to feel followed again in daily life, even when logically she knows no one is there. A car slowing near her as she walks home from the train—she is sure it is tracking her. A person lingering at a bus stop—she interprets it as surveillance. Her negative appraisals shape her perception; because she believes the world is dangerous and people are deceptive, she reads ambiguous cues as evidence of being targeted. This, in turn, feeds additional triggers: each time she feels followed, that feeling itself becomes a trigger, launching another cycle of hypervigilance.

Her maladaptive strategies have become second nature. At work, she scans the studio so relentlessly that she misses conversations around her. She always chooses a seat with a clear sightline to the door, and she plans which way she would run if someone entered with hostile intent. Those very behaviors—the scanning, the planning—keep her in a constant state of alert, making her more reactive to benign sounds and more likely to misinterpret a colleague’s sudden approach as a threat. And they also deepen her conviction that the world is unsafe: if she has to act this way, the danger must be real.

What finally brought her to therapy was an evening walk with her husband. A teenager rode past on a bicycle, and she gasped, grabbed her husband’s arm, and insisted they turn back. She could not explain why a bicycle still terrified her. She knew the stalker was long gone, but the feeling was as vivid as the first day. She is exhausted. She wants to stop scanning, stop flinching, stop believing that everyone around her is a potential predator. But more than anything, she needs to believe that the world can feel safe again, and that the person who hurt her will not continue to control her life from a distance.
